question.text: The NAV computation approach used for fund-level valuation of a Cat II AIF, where each portfolio asset's fair value is aggregated to arrive at the total fund NAV, is called:

explanation.text: **The Logic:** Per PDF Section 11.9: 'This type of valuation is known as the sum of parts valuation method and in AIF parlance, it is known as the BOTTOM-UP APPROACH whereby the NAV of each portfolio asset is added up from bottom to the top as of the valuation date.' **The Trap:** Top-down starts with market cap then allocates — wrong direction; peer-relative is a valuation method not an aggregation approach; exit-waterfall is a distribution concept, not NAV computation. **Cross-Exam Context:** XIX-C tests the same bottom-up principle. Portfolio Manager exams (XXI-B) use identical sum-of-parts for listed portfolios. CFA L3 private markets chapter uses the same nomenclature. **Manager's Pro-Tip:** Your fund administrator should produce a per-asset NAV schedule each valuation date — preserve it as the audit trail. When an LP asks 'how did NAV grow?', you can show which holdings contributed what — this transparency is a common ask in annual LP meetings.
